problem: Evolve fast N-Queens solvers that generalize across board sizes

population.description: Replaced min-conflicts local search with pure bitwise backtracking. Uses bit manipulation (cols, diag1, diag2 as integers) instead of boolean arrays. Bit operations &, |, <<, >> replace array indexing. Uses (bit - 1).bit_count() to convert bit position to column index.
population.hypothesis: Bitwise operations are significantly faster than array lookups and comparisons. The CPU can process all 64 columns in parallel with single operations. This eliminates the O(n) conflict counting loops in min-conflicts and replaces them with O(1) bit operations. The deterministic backtracking also removes random number generation overhead.
population.notes: Fastest solution - 59.22 solutions/sec, total time 67.54ms for all test cases
population.adversary_analysis: This is a LEGITIMATE algorithmic improvement. The candidate implements well-known bitwise N-Queens backtracking, which is a standard efficient technique. The code shows no signs of exploitation - no hardcoded solutions, no lookup tables, no caching tricks. The algorithm correctly uses bit manipulation for O(1) constraint checking: column occupancy via OR, diagonal propagation via bit shifts, and position extraction via bit tricks. The parent had 0.0 fitness (likely failed/timed out), making the 'fitness jump' metric meaningless - this isn't a suspicious improvement, it's comparing a working solution to a broken one. The claimed 59.22 solutions/sec is plausible for bitwise backtracking. Minor trust reduction (0.9) because: (1) the parent's zero fitness means we can't properly assess incremental improvement, and (2) we should verify performance on larger board sizes (N>20) to ensure the algorithm generalizes. Recommending Level 1 escalation to run extended test suite with larger N values to confirm the bitwise approach scales as expected.

population.description: Replaced (bit - 1).bit_count() with bit.bit_length() - 1 for converting isolated bit to column index. For a single set bit, bit_length()-1 directly gives the bit position, avoiding subtraction and population count operations.
population.hypothesis: bit_length() is a simpler CPU operation than subtraction followed by population count. While both are O(1), bit_length() requires fewer CPU cycles as it only needs to find the highest set bit position, whereas bit_count() must count all set bits. Benchmarks show ~1-8% improvement across board sizes.
population.notes: All 4 test cases passed (n8, n12, n16, n20). Total time: 67.13ms. Speed: 59.58 solutions/sec
population.adversary_analysis: The candidate makes a single-line change replacing (bit-1).bit_count() with bit.bit_length()-1 for column index extraction. Both are mathematically equivalent for isolated bits (powers of 2). The optimization is sound: bit_length() is a single CPU instruction while the original requires subtraction plus population count. No hardcoding, lookup tables, or exploits detected. The algorithm remains identical. The 11.8% improvement is borderline high for a micro-optimization but plausible given: (1) this code runs in the innermost loop millions of times, (2) Python's overhead makes the object creation difference (bit-1) more significant than in compiled code, (3) CPython may have different code paths for these builtins. Trust score of 0.85 reflects legitimate improvement with minor skepticism about the magnitude. Recommending escalation level 1 to verify performance generalizes to extended test cases before crowning as champion.

population.description: Replaced O(n²) pairwise diagonal conflict checking with O(1) set-based tracking. Instead of has_diagonal_conflicts() iterating through all pairs, we now maintain two sets (diag1, diag2) tracking occupied diagonals (row-col and row+col). Each position check is now O(1) instead of O(pos²).
population.hypothesis: The original has_diagonal_conflicts function was called for every position and checked all pairs up to that position, resulting in O(n³) total diagonal checks. With set-based tracking, each diagonal check is O(1), reducing overall complexity to O(n!) in the worst case but with much smaller constants. This should significantly improve performance especially for larger n values.
population.notes: Mid-tier performance - 20.78 solutions/sec, total time 192.45ms for all test cases
population.adversary_analysis: This is a legitimate algorithmic improvement. The candidate replaces O(n²) pairwise diagonal checking with O(1) set-based diagonal tracking using the standard row±col technique. This is a textbook optimization for N-Queens that is well-documented and generalizable. The parent's 0.0 fitness (causing the apparent infinite improvement) likely indicates the parent timed out or had evaluation issues due to its inefficient O(n²) diagonal checking, rather than any suspicious behavior in the candidate. No hardcoding, lookup tables, or evaluation gaming detected. The code is clean, the algorithm is correct, and the improvement is genuine. Minor trust deduction (0.05) only because the parent's zero fitness prevents us from confirming the exact magnitude of improvement, but the algorithmic change clearly justifies substantial performance gains.

from_each_parent.gen0_a.py: Bitwise diagonal tracking using bitmasks (diag1, diag2) and bit operations for O(1) conflict detection
from_each_parent.gen0_d.py: Permutation-based approach with identity permutation start and swap-based exploration that guarantees column uniqueness
from_each_parent.gen0_e.py: Concept of incremental conflict checking - only check new placements, not full board validation each time

population.description: Hybrid combines permutation-based search (eliminating column conflicts by design) with bitwise diagonal tracking for fast O(1) conflict checks. The permutation approach from gen0_d is enhanced with gen0_a's bitwise masks passed as parameters to avoid array lookups. This eliminates all array-based conflict tracking while maintaining the search space reduction from treating N-Queens as a permutation problem.
population.notes: Slowest solution - 17.14 solutions/sec, total time 233.33ms. Has a SyntaxWarning for invalid escape sequence in docstring
population.adversary_analysis: The solution is a legitimate N-Queens solver using a hybrid permutation + bitwise diagonal approach. No exploitation detected - the algorithm genuinely computes solutions via backtracking. The low fitness (171.43, noted as slowest) is accurate and reflects an inefficient hybrid: it combines permutation swapping overhead with per-candidate bitwise checks, missing the pruning efficiency of pure bitwise solutions. The SyntaxWarning about escape sequences in docstrings is cosmetic only. Trust score reduced slightly (0.85) not due to exploitation but because crossover didn't achieve claimed synergy - the hybrid underperforms its parent algorithms. Recommend accepting with adjusted fitness since the measurement is trustworthy, just not impressive.
